Least squares is the maximum-likelihood estimate when the noise is Gaussian with constant variance: minimizing the sum of squared residuals is the same as maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood. That link explains both its strengths and its fragility. Squaring means one residual of 10 counts as much as a hundred residuals of 1, so outliers dominate.

Geometrically, the fitted vector y_hat is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X, so the residual vector is perpendicular to every feature column: X^T (y - X w) = 0. Those are exactly the normal equations. Always include an intercept column, otherwise the line is forced through the origin and the residuals no longer average to zero. R^2 = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot measures the share of variance explained, and it never decreases when you add features, which is why adjusted R^2 or held-out error is the honest comparison.

The closed form needs X^T X to be invertible, which fails when features are perfectly collinear or when d > n. Even when it is invertible, forming X^T X squares the condition number, so libraries factor X with QR or SVD instead; numpy.linalg.lstsq and sklearn's LinearRegression use such solvers and return the minimum-norm solution in the rank-deficient case. Ridge regression fixes invertibility outright: w = (X^T X + lambda I)^-1 X^T y.

Cost: forming X^T X is O(n d^2) and solving is O(d^3), cheap for d in the hundreds and painful for d near 10^5. Gradient descent costs O(n d) per pass, and stochastic or mini-batch variants touch a few rows at a time, which suits streaming data and out-of-core training. MSE is convex, so gradient descent reaches the global minimum given a suitable learning rate, but poorly scaled features create elongated valleys and slow, zig-zagging convergence. Standardize first.

Interviewers like the distinction between what is needed for unbiased predictions and what is needed for valid inference. Linearity in the parameters (not the raw inputs: x^2 or log x features are fine) and errors with zero mean given X give unbiased coefficients. Independence and constant variance make ordinary least squares the best linear unbiased estimator (Gauss-Markov). Normality is only needed for exact t-tests and confidence intervals in small samples; with large n the central limit theorem covers it.

Violations have specific fixes. Heteroscedasticity (the funnel): transform the target, use weighted least squares, or report robust (HC) standard errors. Autocorrelated errors in time series: use models that account for it. Multicollinearity does not hurt predictions but inflates coefficient variance; check variance inflation factors (VIF above about 5-10 is a warning) and consider ridge or dropping redundant features. Omitted confounders bias coefficients, which no residual plot reveals.

The sigmoid is the inverse of the logit, so logistic regression assumes the log-odds are linear in the features. Training minimizes the negative log-likelihood, -[y log p + (1 - y) log(1 - p)], which is convex in w, so there is a single global optimum even though no closed form exists. Solvers such as L-BFGS, Newton's method (iteratively reweighted least squares) or SAGA find it. The gradient is beautifully simple: X^T (p - y), the same form as linear regression with p in place of y_hat.

Why not use MSE with a sigmoid? The loss becomes non-convex and gradients vanish when predictions are confidently wrong. For more than two classes, softmax (multinomial) regression generalizes the model with one weight vector per class. The decision boundary is linear in whatever features you feed in, so adding x1^2, x2^2 and x1*x2 produces circles and ellipses while the model stays linear in its parameters.

'Holding other features fixed' is the crucial phrase. With correlated features, a coefficient can shrink, grow or even flip sign when another feature is added, because each weight measures the unique contribution after the others are accounted for. Coefficient magnitude depends on units: a weight per gram is 1000 times smaller than the same effect per kilogram, so standardize before comparing, or report effects for a meaningful change such as an interquartile range.

For logistic regression, e^w is an odds ratio, not a probability ratio. The change in probability from one unit depends on the baseline: near p = 0.5 the slope is w/4 (the 'divide by 4' rule), and near 0 or 1 the same w moves p very little. Interaction terms change interpretation: with x1*x2 included, the effect of x1 depends on x2. Regularized coefficients are shrunk toward zero, so their magnitudes are biased. Causal claims need a design (randomization, instruments or careful adjustment), not just a coefficient.

Checking the numbers: sigmoid(-1) = 1 / (1 + e) = 0.269 and sigmoid(2) = 1 / (1 + e^-2) = 0.881. The boundary solves -4 + 1.5h = 0, so h = 2.67 hours. Notice how the same +1.5 log-odds step moves probability differently along the curve: from 2 to 3 hours p goes 0.27 -> 0.62, a jump of 35 points, while from 4 to 5 hours it goes 0.88 -> 0.97, only 9 points.

In scikit-learn, LogisticRegression applies L2 regularization by default with C = 1.0, where C is the inverse of the penalty strength. That default is helpful for stability but surprises people who expect plain maximum-likelihood estimates; set C=np.inf for an unpenalized fit (penalty=None before version 1.8, which deprecated the penalty argument). predict_proba returns one column per class, so [:, 1] is the positive class. predict uses a 0.5 threshold; for other thresholds compare predict_proba to your own cutoff. Check calibration with a reliability diagram before trusting the probabilities.

Extrapolation: a linear trend fitted on houses from 50 to 200 m^2 says nothing reliable about a 2,000 m^2 mansion, and the prediction interval widens away from the data center. Outliers versus leverage: a point with an extreme x value has high leverage and can pull the line strongly; Cook's distance combines leverage and residual size to flag influential points. Huber loss is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, giving robustness without discarding data.

Perfect separation makes the unpenalized maximum-likelihood weights diverge to infinity, because the loss keeps decreasing as the sigmoid gets steeper; solvers report convergence warnings and huge coefficients. Regularization or Firth's correction fixes it. Class imbalance shifts the intercept and makes 0.5 a poor threshold; choose the threshold from the costs of false positives and false negatives, or use class_weight. Finally, a linear model on raw features may simply underfit nonlinear structure, which shows up as curved residual patterns.

e^0.7 = 2.01, so each unit of x roughly doubles the odds. A good follow-up an interviewer might ask: does it double the probability? Only when the probability is small. Starting from p = 0.1 (odds 0.111), doubled odds give 0.222, so p = 0.18, close to double. Starting from p = 0.6 (odds 1.5), doubled odds give 3.0, so p = 0.75, far from double.

Other quick checks worth being able to answer: what does a negative weight mean (odds shrink, e^-0.7 = 0.50 halves them); what is the intercept (log-odds when all features are zero, which may be meaningless unless features are centered); why can't you read significance from a regularized coefficient (shrinkage biases it and standard errors no longer have their textbook meaning). Explaining the gap between odds and probability clearly is a strong signal in interviews.
ml-classical-01.further: Next steps: generalized linear models (Poisson regression for counts, gamma for positive skewed targets) share the same link-function idea as logistic regression. Learn ridge, lasso and elastic net, and how regularization paths trade bias for variance. Study probability calibration (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) and proper scoring rules such as log loss and the Brier score. For inference, read about robust standard errors and the difference between prediction and causal estimation. Quantile regression predicts conditional medians or percentiles instead of means, useful when costs are asymmetric.

panels:
Trees are built greedily: at each node the algorithm scans every feature and every candidate threshold (midpoints between sorted unique values), picks the split with the largest impurity decrease, and recurses. Finding the globally optimal tree is NP-hard, so greedy search is the standard compromise. For n rows and d features, a naive build costs about O(d n log n) per level after sorting; histogram-based implementations bin features into around 256 buckets to make this much faster.

CART (classification and regression trees), used by scikit-learn, makes binary splits. Regression trees minimize squared error, so each leaf predicts the mean of its rows. Trees are invariant to monotonic transforms of features, which is why scaling does not matter, and they capture interactions naturally because a later split is conditional on earlier ones. Their decision boundaries are axis-aligned rectangles, so a diagonal boundary needs a staircase of many splits. Single trees are unstable: small data changes can produce a very different tree.

Both criteria are concave functions of the class proportions that are zero for pure nodes and maximal for uniform ones. With K classes, maximum Gini is 1 - 1/K and maximum entropy is log2 K bits. Gini is the probability of misclassifying a random sample if you label it randomly according to the node's class distribution; entropy is the expected information needed to identify the class. Empirical studies find they disagree on only a few percent of splits, and Gini avoids computing logarithms.

Why not use plain misclassification error as the split criterion? It is not strictly concave, so many useful splits show zero improvement, which stalls tree growth; it is fine for pruning, though. Information gain is biased toward features with many distinct values, which is why Quinlan introduced the gain ratio (later used in C4.5), normalizing by the split's own entropy. For regression, the analogous criteria are variance reduction (MSE) or absolute error (MAE), the latter being more robust to outliers but slower.

Each child holds 5 of the 10 emails, so weighted child impurity = 0.5 x 0.32 + 0.5 x 0.32 = 0.32, and the gain is 0.5 - 0.32 = 0.18. With entropy instead: parent entropy is 1.0 bit; each child has -(0.8 log2 0.8 + 0.2 log2 0.2) = 0.722 bits; information gain = 1.0 - 0.722 = 0.278 bits. Different scales, same ranking of splits in almost every case.

Weighting by child size matters. A split that peels off one pure email (child of 1 with Gini 0) and leaves 9 mixed ones barely helps: the large child still has Gini close to 0.5. This is why trees with no minimum leaf size happily isolate single points deep in the tree, chasing tiny impurity gains that are really noise. In an interview, being able to compute a split by hand, and explain why the weighted average is used, demonstrates you understand what the library is doing.

An unrestricted tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, which on noisy data means one leaf per training example: zero training error and poor generalization. Pre-pruning stops growth early via max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes or min_impurity_decrease. Post-pruning grows the full tree and then removes subtrees; cost-complexity pruning minimizes error + alpha x (number of leaves), and scikit-learn exposes the sequence of alphas through cost_complexity_pruning_path so you can pick one by cross-validation.

A depth-d binary tree has at most 2^d leaves, so depth 10 already allows 1,024 regions. Depth also bounds interaction order: a depth-3 tree can model at most three-way interactions along a path. This is why boosting uses shallow trees (depth 3 to 8, or 31 to 255 leaves in LightGBM terms) while random forests grow deep trees and rely on averaging to tame the variance. min_samples_leaf is often the most effective single knob for smoothing predictions.

A bootstrap sample draws n rows with replacement, so each tree sees about 63.2% of unique rows (1 - 1/e); the remaining 36.8% are out-of-bag and act as a built-in validation set. Averaging B trees with variance sigma^2 and pairwise correlation rho gives ensemble variance rho sigma^2 + (1 - rho) sigma^2 / B. More trees shrink the second term, but only decorrelation reduces the first, which is why random forests sample features: the default max_features is sqrt(d) for classification, and scikit-learn uses all features for regression (1.0) by default, a common surprise.

Adding trees never causes overfitting in the sense of rising test error; it only stops helping, so a few hundred trees usually suffice. Forests need little tuning, are embarrassingly parallel and give reasonable probability estimates, though often under-confident near 0 and 1. Their main weaknesses are memory and latency with many deep trees, and no extrapolation: predictions are averages of training targets, so a forest cannot predict beyond the range it saw.

Gradient boosting performs gradient descent in function space. At step m it computes the negative gradient of the loss for each training row (for squared error, simply the residual y - F(x)), fits a small regression tree to those values, and adds it scaled by the learning rate: F_m = F_(m-1) + eta x tree_m. Any differentiable loss works, including log loss, Poisson or quantile losses. XGBoost adds a second-order (Newton) step using Hessians plus explicit L1/L2 penalties on leaf weights.

LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise (expanding the leaf with the largest gain) and uses histogram binning, making it very fast; control it with num_leaves and min_child_samples. CatBoost uses symmetric trees and ordered target statistics that avoid target leakage when encoding categoricals. Typical recipe: learning rate 0.01 to 0.1, early stopping on a validation set, row and column subsampling around 0.8, then tune leaves and minimum child size. Smaller learning rates need more trees but generalize better. Boosting reduces bias mainly; it overfits if run too long.

Mean decrease in impurity (MDI) sums the impurity reduction a feature provides across all splits, measured on training data. It inflates features with many split points, such as continuous variables and IDs, and can reward pure noise. Permutation importance shuffles one feature on held-out data and measures the score drop, which reflects real predictive value, but it is unreliable with correlated features: shuffling one creates impossible combinations, and the model can lean on its twin, so both look unimportant.

SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) values distribute each prediction among features according to cooperative game theory; TreeSHAP computes them exactly in polynomial time for trees. They give per-prediction explanations and consistent global rankings, but they still describe the model, not the world. Conditional versus interventional SHAP can disagree when features are correlated. Practical advice: drop or group duplicate features before interpreting, compare multiple methods, and never present importance as causal evidence without an experiment or causal design.

Benchmarks such as Grinsztajn et al. (2022) found tree ensembles beating deep networks on medium-sized tabular datasets (around 10,000 rows) for three reasons: trees are robust to uninformative features, they handle irregular, non-smooth target functions that neural nets with their smoothness bias fit poorly, and they are not rotation invariant, which matters because individual tabular columns carry meaning. Trees also need no feature scaling, cope with missing values natively in XGBoost and LightGBM, and train in minutes on a CPU.

The picture keeps shifting. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN are competitive on small datasets, and neural architectures win when tabular data is combined with text, images or very large datasets with learned embeddings for high-cardinality categories. In industry, gradient boosted trees remain the default baseline for fraud, credit risk, ranking features and churn. A strong answer in interviews: start with LightGBM or XGBoost, then justify any switch with validation results.
ml-classical-02.further: Go deeper with: the original random forest paper (Breiman 2001) and the XGBoost paper (Chen and Guestrin 2016) for the second-order objective. Learn extremely randomized trees (ExtraTrees), isolation forests for anomaly detection, and quantile regression forests for prediction intervals. Study monotonic constraints in boosting libraries for regulated domains, categorical handling in CatBoost, and SHAP interaction values. For model choice, explore stacking (a meta-model over out-of-fold predictions) and tabular foundation models such as TabPFN.

panels:
The hard-margin SVM solves: minimize (1/2)||w||^2 subject to y_i (w.x_i + b) >= 1 for every point, with labels y in {-1, +1}. The margin between the two hyperplanes w.x + b = +1 and -1 is 2/||w||, so minimizing ||w|| maximizes it. This is a convex quadratic program with a unique solution.

In the dual form, the solution is w = sum(alpha_i y_i x_i), and only points with alpha_i > 0 contribute. These are the support vectors, lying on or inside the margin. Removing any other point leaves the boundary unchanged, which gives SVMs some robustness and a sparse model. The maximum-margin principle connects to generalization theory: wider margins mean lower capacity, giving bounds that do not depend directly on the input dimension, which is why linear SVMs work well for high-dimensional text. Note that SVMs output distances, not probabilities; scikit-learn's probability=True runs an extra internal cross-validation with Platt scaling.

The soft-margin problem adds slack variables: minimize (1/2)||w||^2 + C sum(xi_i), with y_i (w.x_i + b) >= 1 - xi_i. Equivalently, minimize the hinge loss max(0, 1 - y f(x)) plus an L2 penalty, so the SVM is just a linear model with a particular loss. C trades margin width against violations; it plays the role of 1/lambda in other regularized models, so large C means weak regularization.

Hinge loss is zero for points correctly classified beyond the margin, so confident correct points do not influence the solution, unlike log loss in logistic regression. Typical tuning searches C on a log scale such as 0.01 to 1000. Imbalanced classes can be handled with class_weight='balanced', which scales C per class. For large linear problems, LinearSVC (liblinear) or SGDClassifier(loss='hinge') scale to millions of rows far better than the kernelized SVC, whose training time grows roughly between O(n^2) and O(n^3).

In the dual, data appears only through dot products x_i . x_j, so replacing them with a kernel k(x_i, x_j) = phi(x_i) . phi(x_j) trains a linear SVM in feature space phi without ever computing phi. A valid kernel must give a positive semi-definite Gram matrix (Mercer's condition). The polynomial kernel (x.x' + c)^d corresponds to all monomials up to degree d; the RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space.

For RBF, gamma sets the reach of each training point: large gamma means very local influence and wiggly boundaries that overfit; small gamma approaches a nearly linear model. scikit-learn's gamma='scale' uses 1 / (n_features x X.var()). Tune C and gamma jointly on a log grid, since they interact. The price: storing and evaluating against support vectors makes prediction cost proportional to their number, and training memory grows with n^2 for the kernel matrix. Approximations such as random Fourier features or Nystroem let a linear model mimic an RBF kernel at scale.

k-NN is a lazy, non-parametric learner: training is just storing the data, and all the work happens at prediction time. Brute-force search costs O(n d) per query; KD-trees and ball trees speed this up in low dimensions (roughly d below 20), and approximate nearest neighbor libraries such as FAISS or HNSW indexes handle millions of high-dimensional vectors, the same machinery behind vector databases for embeddings.

k controls the bias-variance trade-off: k = 1 has zero training error and high variance, while k = n always predicts the majority class. Choose k by cross-validation; a classic heuristic is around sqrt(n). Distance weighting (weights='distance') lets closer neighbors count more. As n grows, the 1-NN error rate is at most twice the Bayes optimal error (Cover and Hart, 1967), a remarkable guarantee for such a simple method. For text embeddings, cosine similarity is standard; for mixed numeric and categorical data, Gower distance is an option. Ties and duplicate points need a deterministic rule.

Distances add squared feature differences, so units decide influence. In the example, an income gap of 1,000 contributes 1,000,000 to the squared distance while a 40-year age gap contributes 1,600: age is effectively invisible. After standardization (say income std 40,000 and age std 15), the same gaps become 0.025 and 2.67 standard deviations, so age now dominates, which matches intuition.

Scaler choice matters: StandardScaler for roughly symmetric data, RobustScaler (median and interquartile range) when outliers exist, and log transforms for heavily skewed counts or money. Fit the scaler on training data only. Beyond scaling, irrelevant features hurt k-NN badly because they add noise to every distance; feature selection or metric learning helps. In high dimensions, the ratio between the nearest and farthest neighbor distances approaches 1 for many data distributions, so neighborhoods stop being meaningful unless data lies on a lower-dimensional structure, which real data often does.

Naive Bayes computes argmax over classes of log P(c) + sum(log P(x_i | c)); working in log space avoids numerical underflow from multiplying hundreds of small probabilities. Variants differ in the likelihood: multinomial NB models word counts, Bernoulli NB models word presence or absence (and penalizes missing words), Gaussian NB assumes each numeric feature is normal within a class, and complement NB is designed for imbalanced text.

Why does a wrong independence assumption still classify well? Classification only needs the correct class to have the highest score, not accurate probabilities; correlated features double-count evidence, pushing scores to extremes, but often in the right direction. That is also why NB probabilities are badly calibrated, clustering near 0 and 1. Naive Bayes is a generative model, learning P(x | c); logistic regression is its discriminative counterpart. Ng and Jordan (2002) showed NB reaches its (higher) asymptotic error faster, so it can win with little data while logistic regression wins with more. Smoothing alpha is a tunable hyperparameter.

Bayes rule: P(spam | free) = P(free | spam) P(spam) / P(free), where P(free) = 0.4 x 0.3 + 0.6 x 0.02 = 0.132. The ratio of likelihoods, 0.3 / 0.02 = 15, is the Bayes factor; it multiplies the prior odds (0.4 / 0.6 = 0.667) to give posterior odds of 10, which is probability 10/11 = 0.91.

With several words, Naive Bayes multiplies their likelihood ratios. If 'meeting' had P(meeting | spam) = 0.01 and P(meeting | ham) = 0.1, its ratio of 0.1 would cut the odds tenfold, back to 1, giving 50%. Laplace smoothing in practice: P(word | class) = (count + 1) / (total words in class + vocabulary size). Without it, a word never seen in ham forces P(ham) to zero regardless of all other evidence. The prior matters too: if spam is actually 90% of traffic in production but 40% in training, the posterior will be miscalibrated until the prior is adjusted.

Rules of thumb. Start with Naive Bayes or a linear model for text, since they train in seconds and give a strong baseline. Use an RBF SVM for small-to-medium dense datasets with complex boundaries, up to tens of thousands of rows. Use linear SVM or logistic regression for large sparse data. Use k-NN when similarity is the natural concept (recommendations, retrieval over embeddings) and you can afford search at query time.

Pitfalls interviewers probe: forgetting scaling for SVM and k-NN; using SVM decision values as probabilities; using k-NN with many irrelevant features; reporting Naive Bayes probabilities as calibrated risks; leaving duplicates that make k-NN look perfect on validation (the nearest neighbor is the same row). On tabular data with mixed types, gradient boosted trees usually beat all three, and on raw text, images or audio, neural models do; these classics remain valuable as fast baselines and interpretable components.
ml-classical-03.further: Explore support vector regression (epsilon-insensitive loss), one-class SVM for novelty detection, and kernel ridge regression and Gaussian processes, which reuse the kernel idea with probabilistic outputs. Learn metric learning and approximate nearest neighbor search (HNSW, IVF-PQ) that power vector search over embeddings. For Bayes, study generative versus discriminative models, Bayesian networks that relax the independence assumption, and calibration methods (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) to fix overconfident probabilities.

panels:
k-means (Lloyd's algorithm) alternates two steps that each can only lower inertia: assignment is optimal for fixed centroids, and the mean is the point minimizing squared distances for fixed assignments. Because inertia never increases and there are finitely many partitions, it always converges, but only to a local minimum. Finding the global optimum is NP-hard. Each iteration costs O(n k d), and it typically converges in tens of iterations.

The implicit model: clusters are spherical, of similar size and variance, because squared Euclidean distance treats all directions equally and boundaries between centroids are straight (a Voronoi partition). k-means is equivalent to a limit of a Gaussian mixture with equal spherical covariances and hard assignments. Mini-batch k-means updates centroids from small random samples, scaling to millions of points with slightly worse inertia. k-medoids uses actual data points as centers and allows any distance metric, which makes it more robust to outliers. Empty clusters can occur and must be reseeded.

First assignment uses midpoint 1.5 between the centroids 1 and 2, so only point 1 joins the first cluster. The second cluster's mean is (2 + 3 + 10 + 11 + 12) / 5 = 38 / 5 = 7.6. The new midpoint is (1 + 7.6) / 2 = 4.3, so 2 and 3 switch clusters. Means become 2 and 11, midpoint 6.5, and nothing moves again. Final inertia: (1 + 0 + 1) + (1 + 0 + 1) = 4.

This trace shows why initialization matters: two adjacent starting centroids made the first step lopsided. Here it recovered, but with more complex data a poor start can leave two centroids sharing one true cluster while another centroid spans two, a local minimum that further iterations never escape. A useful check in interviews is to compute inertia for the final solution and for an alternative partition to show which is better. Ties, where a point is equidistant from two centroids, are broken by a fixed rule such as the lowest index.

k-means++ chooses the first centroid uniformly at random, then each next one with probability proportional to D(x)^2, the squared distance to the nearest centroid already chosen. This spreads starts across the data and gives an expected inertia within O(log k) of optimal, before any Lloyd iterations. It is scikit-learn's default. Even so, run multiple restarts (n_init) and keep the lowest inertia.

Choosing k has no single right answer. The elbow is often ambiguous because inertia always decreases with k. Silhouette for one point uses a = mean distance to its own cluster and b = mean distance to the nearest other cluster; average it over points, and inspect per-cluster silhouette plots for thin or negative clusters. Alternatives: the gap statistic (compares inertia to uniform reference data), the Davies-Bouldin and Calinski-Harabasz indices, BIC for mixture models, and stability across bootstrap resamples. Often the right k is set by the use case, such as how many customer segments marketing can act on.

Agglomerative clustering builds a full merge tree bottom-up. Linkage defines the distance between clusters. Single linkage uses the closest pair and can follow chains, finding elongated shapes but also merging distinct groups through a bridge of points. Complete linkage uses the farthest pair and produces compact clusters but is sensitive to outliers. Average linkage is a compromise. Ward merges the pair that least increases total within-cluster variance, giving k-means-like spherical clusters, and requires Euclidean distance.

Naive cost is O(n^3) time and O(n^2) memory for the distance matrix, so hierarchical clustering is practical up to roughly tens of thousands of points; single linkage can be computed through a minimum spanning tree. Advantages: no need to choose k upfront, any distance metric (except Ward), and an interpretable dendrogram. Large vertical gaps in the dendrogram suggest natural cut heights. Merges are greedy and never undone, so early mistakes persist. Divisive (top-down) clustering exists but is rarer.

DBSCAN labels points as core (at least min_samples points, including itself, within eps), border (within eps of a core point but not core) and noise. Clusters are connected components of core points plus their border points. It finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, determines their number automatically and isolates outliers, labelled -1 in scikit-learn. Border points reachable from two clusters are assigned to whichever is processed first, so results can vary slightly with data order.

Choosing eps: plot each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbor (k = min_samples) in sorted order and pick the knee. A common min_samples heuristic is 2 x dimensions. A single global eps cannot handle clusters of very different densities: either sparse clusters dissolve into noise or dense ones merge. HDBSCAN fixes this by building a hierarchy over all eps values and keeping the most stable clusters, needing mainly a minimum cluster size; it is often the better default. With a spatial index, DBSCAN runs in roughly O(n log n) in low dimensions.

A GMM models the data density as p(x) = sum over k of pi_k N(x | mu_k, Sigma_k), with mixing weights pi_k. EM alternates an E-step, computing responsibilities (the posterior probability that each component generated each point), and an M-step, re-estimating weights, means and covariances from those soft assignments. The likelihood never decreases, but EM converges to local optima and is usually initialized with k-means.

Covariance types trade flexibility for parameters: 'full' (arbitrary ellipses, about d^2/2 parameters per component), 'diag' (axis-aligned ellipses), 'tied' (shared shape) and 'spherical'. Full covariances in high dimensions are expensive and can become singular, which is why regularization (reg_covar) is added to the diagonal. Pick k and covariance type with BIC, which penalizes parameters. Because a GMM is a density model, it also supports anomaly detection (low likelihood points) and sampling new data. Bayesian GMMs with a Dirichlet process prior can switch off unneeded components automatically.

Scaling: k-means, hierarchical and DBSCAN all rely on distances, so one feature in large units dominates; standardize, and consider whether every feature deserves equal weight. Categorical data needs other approaches such as k-modes or Gower distance. High-dimensional data, including raw embeddings, suffers from distance concentration; reduce dimensions first (PCA, or UMAP for density-based methods) or use cosine distance on normalized vectors.

Shape assumptions: k-means and Ward assume convex, similar-size blobs; elongated, nested or crescent shapes need DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, spectral clustering or single linkage. Unequal cluster sizes push k-means boundaries into the larger cluster. Validation is the hardest part, because there is no ground truth; internal metrics such as silhouette favor convex clusters themselves. Check stability across seeds and subsamples, examine cluster profiles, and test whether clusters predict something useful downstream. Remember that clustering is exploratory: the groups are hypotheses, not discoveries, until validated.
ml-classical-04.further: Learn spectral clustering (graph Laplacian eigenvectors, good for non-convex shapes), HDBSCAN, and OPTICS for variable density. Study the evaluation metrics used when labels exist: adjusted Rand index and normalized mutual information. Explore clustering on embeddings from language or vision models, topic modeling (LDA) as soft clustering for text, and anomaly detection methods that build on density, such as isolation forest and local outlier factor. For theory, read about the k-means++ guarantees and EM's connection to variational inference.

panels:
Volume grows exponentially with dimension, so data needed to cover space at fixed density grows exponentially too. A striking fact: in a d-dimensional unit hypercube, the fraction of volume within distance 0.05 of the boundary is 1 - 0.9^d, which is 65% in 10 dimensions and over 99.99% in 100. Almost every point is near an edge, and almost every pair of random points is roughly equally far apart.

For many distributions, the ratio between the farthest and nearest neighbor distance tends to 1 as d grows, which undermines k-NN, kernels with fixed bandwidth and density-based clustering. Rescuing facts: real data usually lies near a much lower-dimensional manifold (the manifold hypothesis), and many features are correlated, so the intrinsic dimension is small. Models with strong inductive biases, regularization and dimensionality reduction exploit this. Interviewers may also ask about the blessing of dimensionality: in high dimensions, classes often become linearly separable, which is why linear models work well on sparse text features.

PCA finds orthogonal directions that maximize projected variance; equivalently, it minimizes the squared reconstruction error of projecting onto k dimensions (the Eckart-Young theorem gives the best rank-k approximation). Computationally, take the SVD of the centered data X = U S V^T: the columns of V are the principal directions, and the variance along component i is s_i^2 / (n - 1). Using SVD avoids forming the covariance matrix and is numerically stabler. Randomized SVD makes PCA fast for large matrices when k is small.

Centering is essential; without it the first component mostly points at the mean. Components are unique only up to sign, so signs can flip between runs or library versions, a common source of confusion when comparing loadings. Projection: Z = (X - mean) V_k; reconstruction: X_hat = Z V_k^T + mean. Variants include incremental PCA for streaming data, kernel PCA for nonlinear structure, sparse PCA for interpretable loadings, and probabilistic PCA, which handles missing values in a principled way.

Shares: 4.0/8 = 50%, 2.5/8 = 31.25%, 1.0/8 = 12.5%, 0.5/8 = 6.25%. Cumulative: 50%, 81.25%, 93.75%, 100%. So keeping 90% needs three components and 95% needs all four in this tiny example. With real data, the spectrum often decays quickly: hundreds of features may compress to a few dozen components.

Ways to choose k: a cumulative variance threshold (90-95% is conventional but arbitrary); the scree plot elbow; Kaiser's rule on standardized data (keep eigenvalues above 1, the average eigenvalue when features have unit variance); cross-validated downstream performance, which is the most defensible when PCA feeds a model. scikit-learn's PCA(n_components=0.95) selects the smallest k reaching 95%. Remember that explained variance is computed on the data PCA was fit on; fit on the training split, then apply the same transform to validation and test, ideally inside a Pipeline so cross-validation stays honest.

Standardization changes the answer: PCA on the covariance matrix favors high-variance features, while PCA on standardized data (the correlation matrix) treats them equally. Neither is universally correct; if all features share meaningful units, such as pixel intensities, raw covariance may be appropriate. Mixed units almost always call for scaling.

Other limits: PCA captures only linear correlations, so a spiral or a curved manifold needs nonlinear methods. It is sensitive to outliers because variance is squared; robust PCA variants help. Maximum variance does not mean maximum relevance for prediction: a low-variance component can carry the label signal, so PCA before a supervised model can discard exactly what you need, while partial least squares or linear discriminant analysis use the labels. Components are linear mixes of all features, which complicates explanations in regulated settings. Finally, PCA assumes numeric data; for categorical data consider multiple correspondence analysis, and for sparse text, truncated SVD (latent semantic analysis) without centering.

t-SNE converts high-dimensional distances into neighbor probabilities with Gaussian kernels whose widths are set per point by perplexity (roughly the effective number of neighbors, typically 5 to 50), then finds a 2D layout whose Student-t neighbor probabilities match by minimizing KL divergence. The heavy-tailed t distribution lets dissimilar points sit far apart, avoiding the crowding problem. The optimization is non-convex and stochastic, so different seeds give different layouts. Barnes-Hut and FFT accelerations make it O(n log n).

UMAP builds a fuzzy k-nearest-neighbor graph and optimizes a low-dimensional layout with a cross-entropy objective; n_neighbors balances local and global structure and min_dist controls how tightly points pack. It is typically much faster than t-SNE and can transform new points, so it is sometimes used as a preprocessing step for clustering (with HDBSCAN), but treat that carefully. Initializing either method with PCA improves global consistency. For many purposes, a PCA plot is the honest first look.

Wattenberg, Viegas and Johnson's 'How to Use t-SNE Effectively' (2016) shows the core traps. Cluster sizes are not meaningful: t-SNE adapts to local density, so a dense tight cluster and a diffuse one can appear the same size. Distances between clusters may mean nothing, and the relative position of islands can change between runs. Random noise with low perplexity can produce apparent clumps. Topology can mislead too: a 3D trefoil knot or nested shapes may be torn apart.

Good practice: run several perplexities and seeds and trust only patterns that persist; color points by known labels or metadata rather than inferring categories from shape; compare with a PCA view; never compute statistics such as cluster distances on the 2D embedding. UMAP preserves global structure somewhat better, but it also distorts densities and distances, and debates continue about how faithfully either method represents global geometry. Treat these plots as hypotheses generators: a striking cluster is a reason to examine the raw features, not a result.

Feature selection keeps original columns, preserving meaning, cheap inference and easier compliance. Filters score features independently of any model (variance threshold, correlation, chi-square, mutual information) and are fast but blind to interactions. Wrappers such as recursive feature elimination or forward selection search subsets using a model, capturing interactions at high compute cost and with risk of overfitting the selection. Embedded methods select during training: L1 penalties, tree-based importance, or gating in neural networks.

Feature extraction creates new features: PCA, truncated SVD for sparse data, independent component analysis for separating mixed signals, autoencoders for nonlinear compression, and pretrained embeddings, which are now the dominant form of extraction for text and images. Extraction usually preserves more information per dimension but loses interpretability. Either way, selection or extraction must be fit inside each cross-validation fold; selecting features on the full dataset and then cross-validating is a classic leakage bug that produces optimistic scores even on pure noise.
ml-classical-05.further: Next topics: linear discriminant analysis (supervised projection that maximizes class separation), independent component analysis, nonnegative matrix factorization for parts-based representations, and random projections (Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma: distances survive projection to O(log n / epsilon^2) dimensions). Study autoencoders and variational autoencoders as nonlinear extraction, intrinsic dimension estimation, and trustworthiness metrics for evaluating embeddings. Read 'How to Use t-SNE Effectively' (Distill, 2016) and the UMAP paper by McInnes et al. (2018).

The diagnostic is the pair of numbers, not either alone. Compare training error with a baseline for what is achievable, such as human-level performance or the Bayes error on the task: the gap between them is avoidable bias. The gap between training and validation error is variance. For example, if humans make 1% error, training is 8% and validation 10%, bias dominates; if training is 1.5% and validation 10%, variance dominates.

Complexity is not just parameter count: feature set, polynomial degree, tree depth, number of boosting rounds, training time and regularization strength all control it. Overfitting can also happen at the level of the whole workflow, when you try many models and pick the best validation score, which is why a final untouched test set matters. Underfitting is sometimes misdiagnosed when the real issue is an optimization failure, such as a learning rate that is too high, so check that training loss actually decreases properly before adding capacity.

For squared loss, with y = f(x) + noise of variance sigma^2, the expected error of a learned model f_hat at x, averaged over training sets, decomposes as (E[f_hat(x)] - f(x))^2 + Var(f_hat(x)) + sigma^2. Bias is how far the average model is from the truth; variance is how much the model changes across training samples; sigma^2 is the irreducible noise, a floor no model can beat. The expectation is over random training sets, which is why variance is a property of the learning procedure, not of one fitted model.

The decomposition is exact for squared error; for 0-1 loss there are only analogous, messier versions. Ensembles target the terms: bagging reduces variance by averaging, boosting reduces bias by adding stages. Regularization accepts a little bias for a large variance reduction. The classic U-curve assumes we increase capacity within a fixed model family; modern overparameterized models complicate it, as the double descent panel describes.

Learning curves answer the most expensive question in practice: will collecting more data help? If training and validation errors have converged at a level that is too high, more data will not help; you need more capacity, better features, or less regularization. If a gap remains and validation error is still falling as data grows, more data is likely to pay off, and extrapolating the curve gives a rough estimate of how much.

Plot them with cross-validation at several training sizes (scikit-learn's learning_curve), and show the spread across folds because small training sizes are noisy. A related tool is the validation curve: error versus one hyperparameter, such as depth or alpha, which displays the U-shape directly. For neural networks, plot error versus epochs as well. Beware of curves where validation is better than training: common causes are dropout or augmentation active only in training, an easier validation set, or leakage. Learning curves for deep models often follow power laws, the basis of scaling laws.

Bayesian view: L2 corresponds to a Gaussian prior on weights and L1 to a Laplace prior, and the penalized solution is the MAP estimate. Geometric view: the constrained problem minimizes loss within a ball; the L1 ball is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes, so the loss contour usually touches it at a corner where some weights are exactly zero. The L2 ball is round, so weights shrink but rarely hit zero.

Ridge has a closed form, w = (X^T X + lambda I)^-1 X^T y, and shrinks weights most along low-variance directions of the data. Lasso has no closed form and is solved by coordinate descent with soft-thresholding. With correlated features, lasso tends to pick one arbitrarily and drop the others, and it selects at most n features when d > n; elastic net (penalty alpha x [l1_ratio x L1 + (1 - l1_ratio)/2 x L2] in scikit-learn) keeps groups of correlated features together. In deep learning, L2 appears as weight decay, which differs from an L2 loss term under Adam, hence AdamW.

This setting, n = 100 and d = 50 with five true signals, is where least squares struggles: with 50 parameters estimated from 100 noisy rows, each coefficient has high variance, and test error can be far above training error. Ridge reduces variance by shrinking all 50 weights, helping prediction but keeping every feature. Lasso shrinks and selects, ideally recovering the five true features, which also makes the model interpretable.

In practice, choose alpha with cross-validation along a regularization path: LassoCV, RidgeCV and ElasticNetCV compute solutions for a grid of alphas efficiently with warm starts. A common choice is the largest alpha within one standard error of the best CV score, giving a simpler model with similar performance. Lasso's selection is not perfectly reliable: correlated features, weak signals and small n cause false inclusions or exclusions, and selected coefficients are biased toward zero. Stability selection (repeated lasso on subsamples) or refitting least squares on the chosen features (relaxed lasso) addresses these. Always standardize features first.

Early stopping treats the number of training iterations as a regularization hyperparameter chosen on validation data. For linear models trained by gradient descent from zero, it is approximately equivalent to L2 regularization, with the effective penalty roughly inversely proportional to the number of steps times the learning rate: weights move along high-curvature directions first and along low-curvature directions only later.

In practice, monitor a validation metric each epoch (or every few hundred steps), keep the best checkpoint, and stop after a patience window, perhaps 5 to 20 epochs for neural networks or 50 to 200 rounds for gradient boosting. Validation loss can be noisy, so smooth it or use a minimum improvement threshold. Two subtleties: the validation set used for stopping is no longer an unbiased estimate of performance, so evaluate on a separate test set; and when you later retrain on train plus validation, you need to scale the number of steps. In large-scale LLM pretraining, models often see each token once, so classic overfitting and early stopping matter less.

Every choice made using a dataset (alpha, feature set, number of epochs, even which model family) leaks a little information from it into the model. Use nested cross-validation or a separate test set to report performance after tuning. Scale features before penalizing: with unscaled data, a feature measured in small units needs a large weight and is penalized heavily, while one in large units escapes, so the penalty encodes arbitrary unit choices.

Naming conventions trip people up. In scikit-learn, Ridge and Lasso use alpha (larger = stronger), while LogisticRegression, LinearSVC and SVC use C = 1/lambda (larger = weaker). Lasso's objective divides the squared error by 2n, so its alpha is not comparable to Ridge's. Other pitfalls: applying weight decay to bias and normalization parameters in neural networks (usually excluded), regularizing one-hot dummy variables unevenly, and assuming regularization can fix label noise or distribution shift. Finally, high variance from too little data is often better solved by collecting data or augmentation than by heavier penalties.

Belkin et al. (2019) and Nakkiran et al. (2019) documented double descent: as model size grows, test error first follows the classic U, then peaks near the interpolation threshold, where the model has just enough capacity to fit the training data exactly, then decreases again in the overparameterized regime. It also appears as a function of training epochs and, counterintuitively, of dataset size: near the threshold, adding data can briefly hurt.

The explanation centers on implicit regularization. Among the many solutions that interpolate the training data, gradient descent tends to find low-norm, smooth ones; at the threshold there is essentially one interpolating solution, and it is forced to fit noise wildly. The peak shrinks or disappears with good explicit regularization and less label noise. Double descent does not overturn the bias-variance decomposition, which still holds; it shows that parameter count is a poor measure of effective complexity. For tabular models of moderate size, the classic trade-off remains the practical guide.
ml-classical-06.further: Learn the 'benign overfitting' literature that explains why interpolating models can generalize, and connect learning curves to neural scaling laws. Study dropout, data augmentation, label smoothing and batch normalization as regularizers in deep learning, and the AdamW paper (Loshchilov and Hutter) on decoupled weight decay. Practice nested cross-validation for honest tuning, and explore Bayesian model selection and information criteria (AIC, BIC) as alternatives to validation-based complexity control.

Scaling matters whenever a method uses distances (k-NN, k-means, SVM with RBF kernels), dot products with penalties (ridge, lasso, logistic regression with regularization), variance (PCA), or gradient descent, where unscaled features create ill-conditioned loss surfaces and slow convergence. Tree-based models split on thresholds and are invariant to any monotonic transform, so scaling is unnecessary.

Standardization does not make data normal; it only shifts and rescales. Min-max scaling is sensitive to outliers, since one extreme value compresses everything else, and test data can fall outside [0, 1]. RobustScaler uses the median and interquartile range. For heavy right skew (income, counts, durations), log1p or a Box-Cox / Yeo-Johnson power transform often helps linear models more than any scaler; QuantileTransformer maps to a uniform or normal distribution at the cost of distorting distances. For sparse data such as TF-IDF, avoid centering, which destroys sparsity; use MaxAbsScaler. Always fit the scaler on training data and reuse its statistics everywhere else.

One-hot encoding creates one binary column per category. For unregularized linear models, drop one column to avoid perfect collinearity with the intercept (the dummy variable trap); with regularization or trees it is fine to keep all. Cardinality is the main constraint: a feature with 50,000 values creates a huge sparse matrix. Options include grouping rare categories into 'other' (min_frequency or max_categories in OneHotEncoder), the hashing trick, target encoding, and learned embeddings in neural networks.

Ordinal encoding imposes an order and equal spacing, which is meaningful for sizes or ratings and misleading for colors or cities in linear models. Trees tolerate arbitrary integer codes better, since they can split repeatedly, though it is still suboptimal. LightGBM and CatBoost handle categorical features natively with specialized split algorithms, and scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting supports categorical_features too. For high-cardinality features in boosting, native handling or carefully cross-fitted target encoding usually beats one-hot.

Target encoding with smoothing: encoding(c) = (n_c x mean_c + m x global_mean) / (n_c + m), where n_c is the category count and m is a smoothing strength. Rare categories shrink toward the global mean; frequent ones keep their own mean. This is a simple empirical Bayes estimate.

The leakage arises because each row's own label contributes to its feature. The model learns to trust the encoding far more than it should, cross-validation looks excellent if encoding happened outside the folds, and performance collapses on new data. The fix is cross-fitting: split training data into K folds and encode each fold using statistics from the other folds only; at prediction time, use statistics from all training data. scikit-learn's TargetEncoder does this cross-fitting internally in fit_transform, which is why fit_transform and fit followed by transform give different results by design. CatBoost's ordered target statistics use a permutation-based variant. For multiclass targets, encode one column per class. Also consider temporal order: encodings should use only past data.

Rubin's taxonomy guides the choice. Missing completely at random (MCAR): missingness is unrelated to anything, so simple imputation adds little bias. Missing at random (MAR): it depends on observed features, so model-based imputation using those features works. Missing not at random (MNAR): it depends on the missing value itself, such as high earners skipping an income question; then the fact of missingness is informative and an indicator column captures it.

Options: mean or median imputation (fast, shrinks variance, distorts correlations), most-frequent or a constant 'missing' category, k-NN imputation, and iterative imputation (IterativeImputer, modeling each feature from the others, similar to MICE). SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True) adds indicator columns automatically. XGBoost, LightGBM and HistGradientBoosting handle NaN natively by learning which branch missing values should take. Never impute the target. Check whether missingness patterns differ between training and production, for example when a form field becomes optional, which silently changes the meaning of the feature.

Kaufman et al. (2012) distinguish two families. Target leakage: features that are consequences of the label or are only recorded after the outcome is known, such as 'refund_issued' for churn, 'took antibiotics' for predicting pneumonia, or a cancellation reason. The test is to ask, for each feature: would I know this value at the exact moment I need the prediction? Train-test contamination: preprocessing, feature selection, oversampling or deduplication done before splitting, or duplicates and related rows (same patient, same user) appearing in both sets.

Temporal leakage is the subtlest: aggregates computed over a window that extends past the prediction time, or random splits on time-series data. Build features as of a cutoff timestamp (point-in-time correct joins, which feature stores support). Detection: suspiciously high scores, one feature with dominant importance, or a model that performs far worse in production than in validation. Adversarial validation, training a classifier to distinguish train from test rows, helps detect distribution differences and contamination.

A Pipeline chains transformers and a final estimator into one object, so cross_val_score, GridSearchCV and model.fit call fit on the transformers using only the current training fold and transform on the validation fold. This removes a whole class of leakage bugs by construction. make_column_transformer routes numeric and categorical columns to different preprocessing; columns not listed are dropped by default (remainder='drop').

The fitted pipeline is the deployable artifact: persist it (joblib or skops) and serving applies exactly the same imputation values, scaling statistics and category vocabulary. Hyperparameters of any step are tunable with the step__param syntax, for example logisticregression__C in a GridSearchCV grid. Use imblearn's Pipeline when resampling such as SMOTE must happen only on training folds. set_output(transform='pandas') keeps column names for debugging, and get_feature_names_out reveals the final feature list. The code on the page uses SimpleImputer with a median strategy, StandardScaler and OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore'), a solid default for mixed tabular data.

Filter methods: VarianceThreshold removes constant or near-constant columns; correlation and mutual information rank features by their relationship to the target, though univariate scores miss interactions (a feature useless alone may be powerful combined with another) and redundancy (two copies of the same signal both score high). Wrapper methods: recursive feature elimination (RFE, RFECV) repeatedly fits a model and drops the weakest features; sequential forward or backward selection adds or removes one at a time. These are expensive and can overfit the selection itself.

Embedded methods: L1 regularization and tree importance select during training; SelectFromModel wraps them. Permutation importance on validation data is a robust check. The critical rule: selection is part of training. Ambroise and McLachlan (2002) showed selecting genes on all data before cross-validation gives near-zero error even on random labels. Put the selector inside the Pipeline. Also question whether selection is needed at all: regularized models and boosted trees often handle many features well, and selection is mostly about cost, latency and interpretability.

High-cardinality identifiers (user IDs, transaction IDs, free-text fields) one-hot encoded create sparse matrices with mostly singleton columns that encourage memorization and fail on new IDs. Either drop them, aggregate behavior per ID into meaningful features, or use embeddings or target statistics. handle_unknown='ignore' turns an unseen category into an all-zero vector; 'infrequent_if_exist' maps it to the infrequent bucket when rare categories were grouped, which is often better. Monitor the rate of unseen categories as a drift signal.

Training-serving skew arises when features are computed by different code paths, for example SQL in batch training and Python in the online service, with subtle differences in time zones, rounding, null handling or aggregation windows. Mitigations: share one feature computation library, log the features actually used at serving time and train on those logs, use feature stores with point-in-time correctness, and add tests that compare offline and online feature values for the same entities. Version pipelines together with models so rollbacks restore both.
ml-classical-08.further: Go further with feature stores and point-in-time joins for production systems, the hashing trick and learned embeddings for high-cardinality categories, and automated feature generation (aggregations over relational data, as in deep feature synthesis). Study time-series features (lags, rolling windows, calendar effects) and the leakage traps they carry. Read Kaufman et al., 'Leakage in Data Mining' (2012), and learn monitoring for data drift and unseen categories after deployment. Explore imbalanced-learn pipelines and scikit-learn's TargetEncoder documentation on cross-fitting.
